newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWB Report-Indicator price down to A$164.75/t.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWB Report-Indicator price down to A$164.75/t.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) indicator price fell by A$5.00 a tonne to A$164.75 during the past week, AWB said in its weekly grain market report.

The AWB said there were reports of wheat crops in the St George area of Queensland where crops had never been grown before, an indication of how difficult it will be to get an accurate assessment of the size of this crop.
The impact of recent frost in Queensland and northern New South Wales was still being assessed, it said.
The AWB wheat crop would be revised on Monday with the latest forecast certain to be above the present estimate of 17.6 million tonnes, it said.
The AWB's existing estimate is less than the 18.8 million tonnes being forecast by the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and higher forecasts by other bodies.
"There were two frosts reported this week in the northern area of NSW which will cause some damage," the AWB said.
New crop wheat prices fell by A$2.00-$3.00 a tonne across the board in the latest week except in South Australia where a A$2.00 a tonne rally occurred in the offer price of Australian Premium White.
Feed grain prices also softned by around A$1.00 a tonne with exception of winter wheat where the price remained firm.
Pulses were unmoved but canola continued to be unpredictable, registering a A$6.50 a tonne rise for the week.
In the United States, confusion still reigned over the potential size of the corn crop with one forecaster this week suggesting production at about 508,000 tonnes above USDA estimates, the AWB said.
The market reacted in the past week to the suspension of the oil-for-food programme for Iraq, the AWB noted.

"While the hope is that the programme will be revived it will delay any sales to Iraq and comes at a time when the International Grains Council boosted its estimate of the world crop by three million tonnes and ABARE and private forecasters lifted Australian estimates considerably," it said.
